content: Acute bronchitis is a self-limiting infection of the lower respiratory tract that primarily affects young children and the elderly, particularly during colder seasons. The most common causative agents are viruses, with influenza being a frequent culprit. The clinical presentation typically includes symptoms such as cough, sputum production, wheezing, and systemic symptoms like fever and malaise. It is essential to distinguish acute bronchitis from other conditions such as pneumonia, asthma, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Management primarily involves reassurance and symptomatic treatment, as antibiotics are generally not indicated. Smoking cessation is particularly effective in reducing the disease's severity and recurrence. Acute bronchitis was first described by Charles Badham in 1808 in England. In 1821, Dr. René Laennec, often referred to as the father of chest medicine, provided a detailed description of the condition. The pathophysiology of acute bronchitis involves the transmission of infectious agents through the large and medium-sized airways, leading to inoculation of the tracheobronchial epithelium. This results in inflammation, thickening of the airway walls, and increased mucus production. Microscopic examination has shown epithelial cell desquamation and denudation down to the basement membrane, accompanied by a lymphocytic cellular infiltrate. The most common causes of acute bronchitis are viral infections, although bacterial pathogens and environmental factors can also contribute. Influenza is a frequent viral cause. In cases of prolonged bronchitis, atypical pathogens such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Bordetella pertussis should be considered. It is also important to rule out pneumonia and atypical pneumonia in such cases. Acute bronchitis must be differentiated from other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, such as pneumonia, asthma, chronic bronchitis, and GERD. This differentiation is critical for appropriate management. In terms of epidemiology, acute bronchitis is the ninth most common reason for outpatient visits in the United States. Its prevalence varies depending on the season, vaccination rates, and the occurrence of outbreaks. It is particularly common among young children and the elderly. Risk factors include age, seasonal variations, and immunization status. The natural history of acute bronchitis is generally favorable. If untreated, the condition typically resolves within two weeks, although symptoms may persist for up to two months in some cases. Most patients recover within 5 to 10 days. However, approximately 20% of patients may experience recurrent episodes in subsequent years. The diagnosis of acute bronchitis is primarily clinical, based on the patient’s history and symptoms. Key symptoms include bronchial irritation (e.g., cough, hoarseness, and sputum production) and systemic symptoms (e.g., chest pain, fever, malaise, and myalgia). On physical examination, findings may include prolonged expiration, wheezing, fever, and abnormal breath sounds. Laboratory tests are rarely necessary but may include serologic tests, viral cultures, or sputum analysis in specific cases. Inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein (CRP) are often elevated, and procalcitonin levels can help differentiate bacterial from non-bacterial causes. Chest X-rays typically show normal findings in cases of acute bronchitis. Treatment of acute bronchitis focuses on reassurance and symptomatic management. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), albuterol, and antitussives may provide symptom relief. Routine use of antibiotics is strongly discouraged. However, in cases caused by atypical pathogens such as Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, or Bordetella pertussis, azithromycin may be prescribed. Primary prevention strategies for acute bronchitis include proper hand hygiene, environmental control, the use of physical barriers, and vaccination against preventable pathogens such as influenza and pertussis.
